summary: AEOLIS is a dark-themed, English-first web app that helps an astronaut plan a safe science EVA on the boxwork unit of lower Mount Sharp, in Gale crater. One pillar is AI climate forecasting: TimesFM 2.5 runs outside the web host on Curiosity's published REMS air-temperature and pressure series and writes precomputed forecasts (horizons of 1, 3, and 7 sols, a q10–q90 uncertainty band, and a Marswalk risk label), which the Climate · AI panel and the helmet HUD display, including the predicted temperature and range. Ridge A, B, and C currently share one Gale series, and a "more CO₂" slider is an educational what-if, not atmospheric physics. The other, equal pillar is a layered NASA map with EVA route planning and safety: Mars Trek imagery, a regional USGS geologic map, a local HiRISE-based elevation model, three walkable routes (Safest, Fastest, and Science), and a traffic-light safety status with rehearsal tools. The helmet HUD joins the two pillars so a crew can carry both the climate outlook and the planned walk from the habitat console onto a phone.
details:
AEOLIS has two equal pillars that meet in a helmet-style heads-up display: AI climate forecasting for the next sols at Gale, and a layered NASA map with EVA route planning and safety tools for a science walk on the boxwork unit of lower Mount Sharp.

AI climate forecasting. TimesFM 2.5 (google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch, Apache-2.0) is run outside the web host, on Colab or a scheduled job, on Curiosity's published REMS air-temperature and pressure series. The app only reads static JSON: a seven-sol horizon with q10, q50, and q90 quantiles. In the Climate · AI tab (and on /climate) the user picks a zone, temperature or pressure, and a 1-, 3-, or 7-sol view, then sees a summary and a Marswalk risk label. A forecast appears only when the model beats persistence; otherwise the measured sol remains the source of truth, and dust opacity is not invented. Risk color follows the forecast temperature change as a planning assumption, not a flight rule. A "What-if: more CO₂" slider (0–50%) applies a simple documented shift (up to +2 K and +10 Pa at +50%) and is labeled an educational simulation, not atmospheric physics. Ridge A, B, and C currently reuse the same Gale series, marked "estimated from Gale." The HUD shows the AI temperature prediction and range beside the walk.

Layered NASA map, route planning, and safety. The same console stacks Mars Trek tiles (MOLA hillshade, Curiosity CTX and HiRISE, day and night THEMIS) with USGS SIM 3292 (regional geologic context only) and a local 4 m DTM from the USGS HiRISE-based Gale DEM, used for slope, hillshade, walk-back envelopes, line-of-sight, and elevation profiles. A planner offers Safest, Fastest, and Science routes among a habitat airlock, a support rover, and boxwork ridges A, B, and C. Suit time, oxygen, battery, and dose are simulated assumptions, not flight rules. A traffic-light Safety panel adds MSL weather, NASA DONKI space weather, and daylight at Gale, with live, rehearsal, and Earth-analog modes and a scenario injector (dust storm, SEP alert, or oxygen leak). The Images tab shows unofficial Curiosity raw images from the boxwork-campaign sols, and Perseverance images for comparison only. Layer controls are inspired by NASA Worldview; no Earth tiles are shown as Mars. Plans can be handed off by QR code, cached offline, or printed as a cue card.

The HUD joins both pillars: few-word EVA guidance plus the AI temperature prediction and range. Built with React, Vite, and Tailwind CSS v4, AEOLIS is English-first, with a Spanish switch and a dark theme. It is a Space Apps prototype, not official NASA procedure. The goal is one honest, hyperlocal picture of a Marswalk, with climate and terrain as equal parts of the same decision.
